items.body:
## Problem

`Petnames::open` (pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/petname.rs:59) replays `petnames.jsonl` through `apply` (petname.rs:196-209), which inserts each `Record::Set` name verbatim. The write path, `Petnames::set` (petname.rs:128-163), refuses:

- names that fail `normalize_name` — empty, longer than 64 chars, or containing control/format (Cf) characters (petname.rs:262-278);
- a name whose `fold` equals another contact's petname for the same owner (Conflict);
- a name whose UTS #39 `skeleton` matches another contact's petname or a directory-alleged account name (the anti-mimicry guard the module doc states as its purpose: "the store refuses a petname that could be taken for someone else's name").

None of those invariants are re-checked at load. A journal written by an older build, a hand edit, a partial restore, or another writer therefore loads state the store itself would never create: two contacts of one owner holding fold-equal petnames (`PayPal` / `paypal`), a petname carrying U+200B, or an 80-char name — and the display/labels path consumes them as if they had passed the guards.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main a51be0e22)

Probe test on the laptop (worktree of origin/main, `cargo test -p id-core --test probe_petname_load`): a hand-written journal with four `set` records — fold-duplicate names for two accounts, a name containing U+200B, and an 80-char name — loads with all four records present verbatim; `Petnames::open` returns Ok.

This is the same shape as #5179 / PR #5190, where `Registry::load` for publications was fixed to validate persisted records against `publish()` invariants at load. The petname store was not covered by that fix. Related audits: #2898 Phase 3 and #4001 both name "directory/petname persistence restores" in their closing-inventory scope — this issue is the concrete, reproduced instance for the petname store and can serve as that inventory's named follow-up for this seam.

Note the deliberate legacy tolerance in the comparison paths (`fold`/`skeleton` strip Cf "so a name stored with one (before they were refused) cannot spoof by the comparison path", petname.rs:236-243): the fix must disposition legacy stored names explicitly — fail-loud like the publications registry, quarantine-with-warning, or normalise — rather than silently breaking existing journals.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Petnames::open` dispositions every replayed `Set` record against the `set()` invariants (normalisability, per-owner fold uniqueness, per-owner skeleton uniqueness), with the chosen behaviour for violations (error naming the line / skip-with-warning / normalise) stated in the module doc.
- [ ] The alleged-name skeleton check that needs directory state is either applied where the directory is available at open time or explicitly documented as a load-time exemption with the reason.
- [ ] Tests: journal with fold-duplicate names, a Cf-carrying name, and an overlong name each produce the documented disposition; a journal written by current `set()` calls reopens unchanged.
- [ ] Existing petname tests stay green (laptop or CI).

🤖 Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A), 2026-11-03.

items.body:
## Summary

`id(petname)`: `Petnames::open` (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`) accepts a **parseable** torn final line — a complete petname record JSON whose trailing newline was lost to a crash mid-append — and the next `commit()` append glues the new record onto that same line. The resulting file can never be opened again: the glued line is unparseable, so `Petnames::open` fails fatally with "petname journal line N is malformed", and because `open_world` propagates that error (`world_store.rs:389`), **the whole world bricks** until someone hand-edits `petnames.jsonl`.

This is exactly the failure #1620 fixed for the envelope outbox ("a parseable torn tail is accepted, then merged into the next record") and #2947 filed for the group log. The sibling rule those fixes established — *an unterminated final line is torn, parseable or not, and is dropped and truncated at open* — was never applied to `Petnames`. #1499 (still open) covers `Petnames` only for the **unparseable** fragment case; its acceptance criteria drop only a final line that is "unterminated **and** unparseable", so a parseable torn tail survives that fix and still glues.

## Evidence (main `106b0571`)

- `Petnames::commit` (petname.rs:184-193) writes one JSON line + `\n` in a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`, so a crash/power loss during that write can leave the full JSON with only its `\n` missing.
- `Petnames::open` (petname.rs:53-79) replays with `text.lines()` (line 63), which yields the final unterminated line like any other; a parseable record is applied via `store.apply(record)` with no completeness check and no truncation/repair — there is no torn-tail handling in the function at all.
- The next `set`/`remove` → `commit()` then appends its line directly after the unterminated one, merging two JSON records onto one line, and reports success.
- On the next open, that merged line fails `serde_json::from_str` and the open returns "petname journal line {N} is malformed". `open_world` (`world_store.rs:389`) propagates the failure, so every world open fails the same way.
- Contrast the established sibling rule: `Outbox::open` (envelope_outbox.rs:141-161) drops an unterminated final line "Parseable or not … Keeping a parseable torn line would let the next append merge two records onto one line and brick the queue (#1620)"; `Directory::replay` (directory.rs, #1521) and `ArtifactLog::open` (artifact.rs) drop and truncate the same way.

## Verified (laptop probe, real `petname.rs`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-petparse/` on the laptop, compiling the **real** `petname.rs` (sha256 `ff6cba651a19ad5814a2540df12433d1444b44ff5fb258a8478cb891be88723e`, identical to the sandbox checkout at main `106b0571`) against a stub `directory::Refusal`; `cargo run` exit 0:

```
control journal bytes: "{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"aa11aa11\",\"name\":\"Ali\"}\n"
CONTROL clean journal: open OK, Ali=Some("Ali")
PARSEABLE TORN TAIL: open OK, Carol=Some("Carol") (accepted despite no newline)
AFTER NEXT APPEND bytes: "{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"aa11aa11\",\"name\":\"Ali\"}\n{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"cc33cc33\",\"name\":\"Carol\"}{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"dd44dd44\",\"name\":\"Dave\"}\n"
REOPEN AFTER APPEND: open FAILED: petname journal line 2 is malformed: trailing characters at line 1 column 64
```

- Control: a healthy newline-terminated journal opens and replays.
- Case: after appending a complete record with only its trailing `\n` stripped (the crash cut), reopen **accepts** Carol; the next `set` (Dave) succeeds but glues onto Carol's line; the final reopen is **bricked**.

## Why it matters

`petnames.jsonl` is a small private store, but `open_world` loads it on the world-open path, so one unlucky crash during a petname rename converts a recoverable one-byte tear into a permanently unopenable world on the next ordinary write — silently (the append reports success). Three sibling stores in the same crate already encode the correct rule with regression tests; `Petnames` is the remaining store that doesn't, and the open #1499 fix as scoped does not close this parseable half.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Petnames::open` treats an unterminated final line as torn **whether or not it parses**: the line is dropped and the file is truncated to the last complete line — mirroring `Outbox::open` (#1620) — ideally coordinated with the #1499 fix so both torn cases land in one replay rewrite (`split_inclusive('\n')`).
- [ ] Regression test in `petname.rs` mirroring the outbox's `a_parseable_torn_last_line_is_also_dropped`: write a valid record, strip only its trailing newline, reopen (record dropped, file truncated), set a new petname, reopen again and replay successfully.
- [ ] Existing behavior unchanged: a newline-terminated line that does not parse stays fatal with the line-numbered error; blank lines still skipped; healthy journals set/remove/reopen exactly as before.
- [ ] Related, do not duplicate: #1499 (Petnames unparseable torn tail — open; this is its parseable sibling case), #2947 (group log parseable torn tail — open, same pattern), #1620 (outbox parseable torn tail — closed), #1521 (directory torn tail — closed).

# id: a torn final line in petnames.jsonl bricks the whole world — Petnames::open refuses a crash-torn tail that FileJournal and Outbox both drop and truncate

## Summary

`Petnames::open` (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:56-70`) replays `petnames.jsonl` with `text.lines()` and fails the entire open on **any** malformed line — including a torn final line left by a crash mid-append. `Petnames::commit` (`petname.rs:186-199`) appends one JSON line + `sync_data()` per change, so a crash or power loss during `write_all` leaves exactly that: a partial JSON record with no trailing newline at the tail of the file.

That failure is not contained to petnames. `open_world` (`pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:389-392`) propagates it with `??`, so **the whole world fails to open** — on every restart, forever, until someone hand-edits the journal. There is no recovery path: appends can't happen because open never succeeds.

The two sibling JSONL stores loaded by the same `open_world` already handle this exact case, deliberately:

- **FileJournal** (`world_store.rs:52-117`): "A torn final line, left by a crash mid-append, is truncated away" — unterminated last line is dropped, the file is truncated to the last good byte, and mid-file corruption is still refused. Test: `torn_final_entry_is_dropped_but_mid_file_corruption_is_refused` (`world_store.rs:1044`).
- **Outbox** (`envelope_outbox.rs:141-161`): iterates `split_inclusive('\n')`; an unparseable line that does not end with `'\n'` ends the replay, and the file is truncated to the kept prefix. Test: `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record` (`envelope_outbox.rs:523`).

`Petnames` (and `Directory::replay`, `directory.rs:517-535` — same strict `lines()` + `?` shape, also propagated by `open_world` at `world_store.rs:385-387`) never got the same treatment.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 67e0def2)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-petname`) compiling the **real** `petname.rs` (sha256 `ff6cba651a19ad5814a2540df12433d1444b44ff5fb258a8478cb891be88723e`, identical to the checkout) against a stub `directory::Refusal`:

- Control — clean journal (two records written through `Petnames::set` itself): open OK, both names replay.
- **Torn tail** — the same bytes plus a partial record `{"op":"set","owner":"00ff","account":"cc33","name":"Car` (no trailing newline): `open FAILED: petname journal line 3 is malformed: EOF while parsing a string at line 1 column 55`.
- Control — malformed line in the **middle** (newline-terminated, valid record after it): open FAILED, as it should — mid-file corruption must stay refused.

Log: goal bookkeeping `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-petname/out.log`.

## Why it matters

Petnames are a small, private, append-only store; losing the ability to open them should never take down an entire world. Today one unlucky crash during a rename makes the world permanently unopenable without manual file surgery — while the world's main journal and its outbox, loaded seconds earlier in the same function, already survive the identical failure by design.

## Fix direction

Bring `Petnames::open` in line with the house pattern (Outbox is the closest model — same one-record-per-line JSONL, same append commit):

- Replay with `split_inclusive('\n')`; a final line that is unterminated **and** unparseable is a torn append: drop it and truncate the file to the kept prefix (so the next append is not glued onto the partial record — the failure the Outbox test name calls out).
- Any other malformed line (terminated, or mid-file) stays a hard error, exactly as today.
- Consider the same treatment for `Directory::replay` in the same pass — it is the other strict replay on the `open_world` path; if it is deliberately out of scope, say so on the issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `petnames.jsonl` whose final line is a partial JSON record (no trailing newline) opens successfully with all complete records replayed; the torn bytes are truncated from the file.
- [ ] After such a recovery, a subsequent `set`/`remove` appends a clean record that replays correctly on the next open (no gluing onto the torn bytes).
- [ ] A malformed line anywhere else (newline-terminated, or followed by more records) still fails the open with the line-numbered error.
- [ ] The existing test `a_malformed_line_fails_the_open` is updated/narrowed to the mid-file case, and a new test mirrors `torn_final_entry_is_dropped_but_mid_file_corruption_is_refused` for petnames.
- [ ] `cargo test` for the petname module passes; behaviour of clean journals is unchanged.

items.body:
## Problem

Every JSONL journal loader in pkgs/id that promises crash-torn-tail tolerance reads the whole file with `std::fs::read_to_string` **before** its torn-tail logic runs. `read_to_string` fails on any invalid UTF-8 anywhere in the file, so a crash that tears an append **in the middle of a multibyte character** (a name containing `é`, an emoji, CJK text — all legal in these journals) bricks the open entirely: the loader returns the UTF-8 error instead of dropping and truncating the torn final line as its own doc promises. The complete, valid records before the tail are unreachable.

Affected loaders (all verified at the lines below on current main):

- `crates/id-core/src/petname.rs:64` — `Petnames::open`: doc (lines 54–58) promises a torn final line "is dropped and truncated away"; the `read_to_string` at :64 errors first.
- `src/groups/log.rs:56` — `GroupLog::open`: same promise (doc lines 44–50), same `read_to_string` first.
- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:135` — `Outbox::open`: torn-tail handling at :143–175 is unreachable for a UTF-8-split tail.
- `src/artifact.rs:579` — `ArtifactLog::open`: doc (lines 573–576) promises a crash-cut final line "is dropped and the file is truncated"; `read_to_string` at :579 errors first.
- `src/directory.rs:494` — `Directory::replay`: the #1521 torn-tail repair computes `kept_len` from the string it already failed to read.

The world journal in the same codebase does this correctly: `FileJournal::open` (`src/world_store.rs:59`) reads bytes with `read_until(b'\n')` and parses with `serde_json::from_slice`, and `read_journal_entries` (`src/world_store.rs:466`) splits the raw bytes on `b'\n'` — a UTF-8-split torn tail is dropped there exactly as documented.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-utf8torn`, at GitHub main 9f096d925; all five loader sources md5-matched between the sandbox and laptop clones): an integration test against the real `id_core::petname::Petnames`:

- Control: a valid journal plus an ASCII torn tail (no newline) reopens fine — the existing torn-tail path works for ASCII.
- Probe: a valid journal whose first record sets the petname `José`, followed by a torn second record cut after the first byte (`0xC3`) of an `é` in the name, with no trailing newline — `Petnames::open` FAILS instead of dropping the tail and keeping `José`.

Probe output (`cargo test -p id-core --test probe_utf8_torn -- --nocapture`):

```
CONTROL ascii torn tail: OK (dropped, Ali kept)
test control_ascii_torn_tail_is_dropped ... ok
PROBE utf8-split torn tail: open FAILED: stream did not contain valid UTF-8
test probe_utf8_split_torn_tail ... FAILED (BUG REPRODUCED: utf8-split torn tail bricks Petnames::open)
```

The other four loaders share the identical construction (`read_to_string` returning the same std UTF-8 error before any line logic), so the same torn file bricks each of them; the probe exercises the petname loader against the real crate code as the representative case.

Earlier torn-tail fixes — #1499/#2948 (petnames), #1521 (directory), #1522 (groups), #1620/#2150 (outbox), #2128 (artifacts) — each tested torn tails made of ASCII or complete characters, so this sub-case survived all of them.

## Why it matters

These journals are the durable state of a world (directory, groups, outbox, artifacts, petnames). One crash at the wrong byte turns a recoverable, documented torn tail into a world that will not open at all, with an error ("stream did not contain valid UTF-8") that does not name the torn tail — the exact failure class the torn-tail fixes were written to eliminate, gated on whether the torn record happened to contain non-ASCII text.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each affected loader reads bytes (or otherwise tolerates invalid UTF-8 confined to the unterminated final line), drops and truncates a torn final line even when it splits a multibyte character, and reopens with all complete records intact.
- [ ] A newline-terminated line containing invalid UTF-8 / unparseable content in any earlier position still fails the open as corruption (the torn-tail tolerance must not widen).
- [ ] Regression tests for each fixed loader: valid record with a non-ASCII name + a final line torn mid-character reopens with the valid records and the file truncated to the last complete line; the next append after reopen replays cleanly.
- [ ] Existing torn-tail and journal tests for petnames, groups, outbox, artifacts and directory still pass.

# id(petname): skeleton confusable check is ASCII-only — Cyrillic/Greek homoglyph petnames pass the anti-mimicry guard and render with no fingerprint

## Summary

`Petnames::set` refuses a petname that is confusable with another contact's petname or alleged name, comparing `fold()` and `skeleton()` forms (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:113-135`). The design decision is "Mimicry: refuse, for both exact (folded) and confusable matches" (`pkgs/id/docs/2026-10-10T07-00-00Z_feature_petnames_invites/2026-10-10T07-00-00Z_feature_petnames_invites.md`, Decisions). But `skeleton()` (`petname.rs:240-257`) maps only ASCII look-alikes (`0→o`, `1→l`, `|→l`, `3→e`, `5/$→s`, `@→a`, `rn→m`, `vv→w`). `normalize_name` (`petname.rs:217-231`) admits any non-control characters, so a petname or alleged name written with Cyrillic or Greek homoglyphs — visually identical in the terminal and web UI — produces a different skeleton and is accepted:

- "PayP**а**l" with U+0430 (Cyrillic small a) vs "PayPal"
- "**А**lice" with U+0410 (folds to U+0430, still not Latin `a`)
- "B**о**b" with U+043E, "**е**ve" with U+0435, "**С**arol" with U+0421, "T**ο**m" with U+03BF (Greek omicron)

Display does not rescue it: `labels()` (`petname.rs:311-330`) adds the disambiguating fingerprint only when two petnames collide after `fold()` — fold also differs for these pairs, so both contacts render bare, visually identical, with no fingerprint.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `ffa86396`)

Verbatim-copy probe of `fold`/`skeleton` (`petname.rs:233-257`), compiled with rustc and run on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-petuni/`:

```text
control "PayPal" vs "PayPa1": skeleton_eq=true   (refused today, as designed)
control "PayPal" vs "paypa1": skeleton_eq=true   (refused today)
control "Mum" vs "rnurn":     skeleton_eq=true   (refused today)
homoglyph "PayPal" vs "PayPаl" (U+0430): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false  skeleton_b="paypаl"
homoglyph "Alice"  vs "Аlice"  (U+0410): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Bob"    vs "Bоb"    (U+043E): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Eve"    vs "еve"    (U+0435): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Carol"  vs "Сarol"  (U+0421): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Tom"    vs "Tοm"    (U+03BF): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
```

`set()`'s only confusable checks are those two equalities (petname.rs:120, :128), so every homoglyph case above is accepted today, for both the existing-petname comparison and the alleged-name comparison.

Related but distinct: #2069 (skeleton misses ASCII `I`/`l` and `8`/`B` — two map entries), #1674 (Cf format characters bypassing the guards). This issue is the cross-script class: the fix shape is a Unicode confusable skeleton (e.g. UTS #39 confusables) and/or a mixed-script rule, not two more ASCII entries. Triage may fold this into #2069 if it prefers one skeleton-hardening item — the acceptance criteria below are written to survive either way.

## Why it matters

The petname store is a trust surface: a name the owner sees must not be taken for a different contact (module doc, `petname.rs:1-6`). Cross-script homoglyphs are the standard, best-known way to defeat exactly this kind of check, they need no invisible characters (#1674's class), and the resulting pair of contacts renders with no fingerprint to tell them apart — a wrong-identity steer for messages or payments to the wrong account key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skeleton()` (or its replacement) equates the common cross-script confusables: at minimum Cyrillic а/е/о/р/с/х/у and А/В/Е/К/М/Н/О/Р/С/Т/Х and Greek ο/ν/ρ/τ/χ look-alikes with their Latin counterparts, so `Petnames::set` refuses the six verified cases above (against both an existing petname and an alleged name).
- [ ] Alternatively/additionally, a documented mixed-script rule: a petname mixing Latin with Cyrillic/Greek letters is refused or skeleton-normalized — whichever shape triage pins, the six cases above must not be silently accepted.
- [ ] Legitimate non-Latin names are not broken wholesale: a petname written entirely in one non-Latin script (e.g. a genuinely Cyrillic name with no Latin look-alike target) still works, or its refusal is an explicit, documented decision.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing petname tests: homoglyph-vs-petname refused, homoglyph-vs-alleged refused, ASCII controls (`PayPa1`, `rnurn`) still refused, unrelated names still accepted.
- [ ] If triage folds this into #2069, close as duplicate pointing there and extend #2069's criteria with the cases above rather than dropping them.

# id(petname): skeleton look-alike map misses capital `I` (vs `l`) and `8` (vs `B`) — "PayPaI" and "8ob" pass the anti-spoof guard that refuses "PayPa1" and "B0b"

## Summary

`Petnames::set` refuses a petname that is confusable with another contact's
petname or alleged name, comparing `skeleton()` forms (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:120`
and `:128`). The skeleton's look-alike table (`petname.rs:240-256`) maps
`0→o`, `1→l`, `|→l`, `3→e`, `5→s`, `$→s`, `@→a`, plus `rn→m` and `vv→w` — but
two classic look-alikes are missing:

- **Capital `I` for `l`.** `fold()` lowercases first, so `I` becomes `i`,
  not `l`. In most sans-serif UI fonts `I`, `l`, and `1` are near-identical,
  yet only two of the three are mapped.
- **`8` for `B`.** The digit look-alikes `0`, `1`, `3`, `5` are all mapped;
  `8` is not.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0fda29d1`)

Verbatim-copy probe of `fold`/`skeleton` (`petname.rs:233-256`), compiled and
run on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-skeleton/`:

```text
skeleton("PayPa1")="paypal"  skeleton("PayPal")="paypal"  equal=true   (refused today)
skeleton("PayPaI")="paypai"  skeleton("PayPal")="paypal"  equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("AIice") ="aiice"   skeleton("Alice") ="alice"   equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("8ob")   ="8ob"     skeleton("Bob")   ="bob"     equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("B0b")   ="bob"     skeleton("Bob")   ="bob"     equal=true   (refused today)
controls: "M0m"/"Mom", "vvill"/"will", "Rnoon"/"moon" all equal, as designed

set(other, "PayPa1") vs alleged "PayPal": refused_by_guard=true
set(other, "PayPaI") vs alleged "PayPal": refused_by_guard=false
set(other, "8ob")    vs alleged "Bob":    refused_by_guard=false
```

So an owner can be talked into (or a crafted flow can set) a petname for one
contact that reads as another contact's name — exactly the spoof the module
exists to prevent ("Account names are alleged, so the store refuses a petname
that could be taken for someone else's name", `petname.rs:1-6`).

Display does not rescue it: `labels()` (`petname.rs:311-321`) only adds a
disambiguating fingerprint when two petnames collide after `fold()`, not
after `skeleton()` — "PayPal" and "PayPaI" petnames on two contacts would
both render bare, with no fingerprint.

Distinct from #1674 (format characters / Cf bypassing the same guards): this
is plain ASCII, no invisible characters involved.

## Why it matters

The petname store is a trust surface: its one job is that a name the owner
sees cannot be mistaken for a different contact. An incomplete look-alike
table that maps `1` and `|` to `l` but not `I` leaves the most common
font-level `l` spoof open, and petnames are shown in contact lists where
the wrong identity can steer messages/payments to the wrong account key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skeleton("PayPaI") == skeleton("PayPal")` and
      `skeleton("AIice") == skeleton("Alice")`: capital `I` maps to the
      same class as `l`/`1`/`|`.
- [ ] `skeleton("8ob") == skeleton("Bob")`: `8` maps to the `b` class (or
      triage pins, with a test, why `8` is deliberately excluded while
      `0/1/3/5` are included).
- [ ] `Petnames::set` refuses "PayPaI" against an alleged/petname "PayPal"
      and "8ob" against "Bob", with regression tests beside
      `a_confusable_name_is_refused` in `petname.rs`.
- [ ] Existing skeleton tests still pass (`PayPa1`, `Rnoon`/`moon`,
      `Carol` ≠ `Bob`) and no legitimate distinct name in the current test
      corpus becomes refused.
- [ ] Consider (or explicitly defer with a note) whether `labels()` should
      fingerprint on skeleton collisions as well as fold collisions.

## Finding

`pkgs/id` durable worlds live in a CWD-relative `.id-worlds/<NAME>/` directory that is gitignored nowhere. Running `id serve` with a world from inside a repo checkout creates `.id-worlds/<name>/` in the checkout, and most of its contents — the world's journal, directory, petnames, mail outbox, installed modules and records namespace — show up in `git status`, one `git add -A` from being committed. This is the same failure #420 and #432 fixed for the identity DB and for `events.redb`/`groups.jsonl`; the world directory as a whole was missed, and only two of its files happen to be covered by those basename fixes.

## Evidence (verified on current main `d3bba2d3`)

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:408,416-418`: `pub const WORLDS_DIR: &str = ".id-worlds";` and `world_dir(name)` returns `PathBuf::from(WORLDS_DIR).join(name)` — relative, no data-dir prefix of its own.
- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:82-87` (comment + code): all data paths are CWD-relative; the process only changes directory when `--data-dir` or `--new` is given. A plain `id serve` from a checkout therefore writes `.id-worlds/` into the checkout. `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:387` documents: "The world's files live in `.id-worlds/<NAME>/`."
- World directory contents: `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:321-346` opens `journal.jsonl`, `directory.jsonl`, `petnames.jsonl`, `outbox.jsonl` and `modules/<blake3>.wasm` under the world dir; `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:50` puts `artifacts.jsonl` beside `directory.jsonl`; `serve.rs` (~line 574) adds `records.namespace`; the event store and group log add `events.redb` / `groups.jsonl`.
- `git check-ignore` on main `d3bba2d3` — none of these is ignored:
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/journal.jsonl` -> NOT IGNORED
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/directory.jsonl` -> NOT IGNORED
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/artifacts.jsonl` -> NOT IGNORED
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/petnames.jsonl` / `outbox.jsonl` -> NOT IGNORED
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/records.namespace` -> NOT IGNORED
  - `.id-worlds/lobby/modules/abc.wasm` -> NOT IGNORED
  - Only `events.redb` (root `.gitignore:120`) and `groups.jsonl` (`:122`) are covered, by the repo-wide basename rules from #432. Root `.gitignore:117-122` has `.iroh*`, `.identity.db`, `.identity.redb`, `events.redb`, `events.redb.tmp`, `groups.jsonl` — no `.id-worlds`.
- Dedup: `gh search issues "id-worlds"` returns nothing; #420/#432 cover different files and are closed.

## Why it matters

A world's journal and directory are the world's durable state (inputs, installs, directory records, petnames, queued mail). Committing them by accident leaks that state into git history and bloats the repo with append-only logs and wasm modules — exactly the accident class #372/#420/#432 already had to clean up for the identity DB and event store. The partial coverage is worse than none in one way: `git status` still shows the directory, so the remaining files look deliberately tracked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root `.gitignore` ignores `.id-worlds/` at any depth (mirroring the repo-wide `.iroh*` / `events.redb` entries from #420/#432), so `git check-ignore .id-worlds/<any>/journal.jsonl` (and `directory.jsonl`, `artifacts.jsonl`, `petnames.jsonl`, `outbox.jsonl`, `records.namespace`, `modules/*.wasm`) succeeds.
- [ ] No tracked file lives under a `.id-worlds/` path (verify with `git ls-files | grep id-worlds` — expected empty), so no `git rm --cached` is needed; if one exists, remove it from tracking in the same change.
- [ ] The existing id entries (`.identity.db`, `.identity.redb`, `events.redb`, `groups.jsonl`) are unchanged.

Suggested fix: add `.id-worlds/` to the root `.gitignore` id block next to `.iroh*`.

## Summary

In `pkgs/id/src/references.rs` (the #2259 friendly-name PoC), the Tier-1 petname match in `LocalIndex::best_match` hardcodes `ClaimState::Uncontested`, and the `claimants()` helper that computes contested state counts only titles and alias claims — never petnames. `LocalIndex::set_petname` also places no uniqueness constraint on the name: the petname map is keyed by target, so one viewer can give two different actors the same petname.

Result: when two actor targets share one viewer petname, `resolve` returns both as Tier-1 `MatchKind::Petname` candidates whose provenance both claim `ClaimState::Uncontested`, and `Resolution::is_contested()` returns `false`. That contradicts the module's own stated rule (module docs): "A surface claimed by two or more targets is **contested**: every candidate is shown with its provenance and nothing is picked silently." The exact-claim and exact-title tiers do compute the state through `claim_state()`/`claimants()`; only the petname tier bypasses it.

The auto-pick itself is safe — the top-tier tie makes `Resolution::single()` return `None`, so `insert_unambiguous` still refuses. What is wrong is the provenance every consumer reads: `Candidate::contested()` and `Resolution::is_contested()` both report "no contest here", so a UI or caller that warns on contested surfaces (the reason `ClaimState` exists) stays silent for exactly the viewer's own names, the tier ranked most trustworthy.

Relevant code (main `b3eb4ef8a`, `pkgs/id/src/references.rs`):

- `set_petname` (:348-350): inserts into `petnames: BTreeMap<Hash, String>` keyed by target — duplicate names across targets are accepted.
- `claimants` (:382-396): counts objects of the sigil whose **title or alias claims** fold-equal the surface; petnames are not counted.
- `best_match` Tier 1 (:446-456): on a petname match returns `candidate(MatchKind::Petname, petname.clone(), object.author, ClaimState::Uncontested)` — the state is a literal, never computed.
- Contrast Tier 2 (:458-470): `ExactClaim`/`ExactTitle` pass `claim_state(&claim.text)` / `claim_state(&object.title)`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-petname-contested/` — verbatim `references.rs` from origin/main `b3eb4ef8a` (pristine md5 `1a64cc11233f79484159fc53cf53ea23`; the probe copy differs by exactly one line, the `p2panda_core::Hash` import swapped for a deterministic stub with the same API, md5 `9be8f7cc3866c7109f2a3769a753601a`). The module's own 14 tests all pass in the probe. Three added probe tests (`tests/petname_contested.rs`):

```
shared_petname_candidates_are_both_marked_uncontested ... ok
  — two live actors, viewer petname "ann" set on BOTH: resolve(Actor, "ann")
    returns 2 candidates, both MatchKind::Petname, both
    provenance.claim_state == Uncontested; is_contested() == false;
    single() is None (the tie alone blocks the auto-pick).
control_shared_title_candidates_are_marked_contested ... ok
  — control: two actors titled "Minutes" both get ClaimState::Contested
    and is_contested() == true, so the claimants path works for titles.
control_single_petname_is_uncontested_and_pickable ... ok
  — control: one actor with petname "ann" resolves Uncontested and
    single() returns it (existing intended behavior, references.rs:648ff).
```

## Why it matters

`ClaimState` is the signal the design gives an author that a surface needs a second look before a reference is committed (`Provenance` docs: "enough for the author to tell duplicates apart and to judge a claim"). A shared petname is precisely a duplicate surface — and petnames are viewer-private, so no one else can see the collision coming. The codebase already treats set-time refusal as insufficient elsewhere: `petname.rs`'s `labels()` adds fingerprints for legacy stored names that `set` would now refuse (#2069), because stored state outlives the guard. `LocalIndex` has no set-time guard at all, so the resolve-time state is the only line of defence, and it currently always says "uncontested" for the petname tier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When two or more actor targets share the viewer's petname (folded comparison, as all tiers fold), their Tier-1 candidates carry `ClaimState::Contested` and `Resolution::is_contested()` returns `true`.
- [ ] A petname held by exactly one target still resolves `ClaimState::Uncontested` and remains auto-pickable via `single()` / `insert_unambiguous` (existing test `petname_outranks_an_exact_claim_for_actors` still passes).
- [ ] The rule is implemented in one place (e.g. `claimants` also counts petname holders for the actor sigil, and the petname tier uses `claim_state()` like Tier 2) rather than a second ad-hoc counter; module docs state the outcome.
- [ ] New tests cover: shared petname → both candidates contested; shared petname where one holder is a topic (sigils do not cross — topics have no petname tier, so no contest); the module's existing tests still pass.

Distinct from: #4455 (same module: `resolve` ignores the `cleared` flag — this issue is about live targets and the petname tier's claim state, and remains after a cleared-filter fix), #2259 (the PoC tracker this module implements), #2069 / `petname.rs` (the replicated petname store's own conflict refusal — `LocalIndex::set_petname` is a separate in-memory API with no such refusal).

`pkgs/id` petnames exist so a contact can never be mistaken for someone else: the module doc (`src/petname.rs:1-7`) says the store "refuses a petname that could be taken for someone else's name", and `normalize_name` promises a petname "cannot contain control characters". Both promises are defeated by Unicode **format characters (general category Cf)**:

- `normalize_name` (`src/petname.rs:217-230`) refuses a name when `name.chars().any(char::is_control)`. Rust's `char::is_control` is category **Cc only**. Category-Cf characters — U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+2060 WORD JOINER, U+FEFF, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN — pass.
- `set()`'s confusability checks (`src/petname.rs:107-135`) compare `fold()` (lowercase) and `skeleton()` (look-alike map + `rn`→`m`, `vv`→`w`) verbatim. Neither strips Cf characters, so an invisible suffix changes both strings while changing nothing on screen.

## Verified shapes (main `d39e6111`, `src/petname.rs` sha256 `ff6cba65`)

Premise exercised this run with a faithful mirror of `normalize_name`/`fold`/`skeleton`/`set` (probe folder: `probe-2026-10-28-laneB-petnamecf/premise.py` + `premise.log`):

- CTRL: `Pay<TAB>Pal` → refused by normalize (Cc). `PayPa1` vs alleged `PayPal` → refused as confusable. Both guards work for the shapes they cover.
- **BUG-A (spoof):** petname `PayPal` + U+200B for a *different* contact, while another contact's alleged name is `PayPal` → **ACCEPTED** (`fold` unequal, `skeleton` unequal). The two names render identically in the directory view (`src/directory_view.rs` builds its labels from `petname::labels`), so the viewer sees two contacts apparently named exactly "PayPal" — precisely the impersonation shape the module exists to prevent.
- **BUG-B (bidi):** a petname containing U+202E is **ACCEPTED** by `normalize_name`, despite its documented "cannot contain control characters" rule. A right-to-left override in a displayed label (`Label::text`, `src/petname.rs:285-295`) can reorder the visible text around it.
- **BUG-C:** `PayPal` + U+2060 WORD JOINER → also ACCEPTED against alleged `PayPal`.

Existing tests (`src/petname.rs` `mod tests`) pin the Cc tab case and the `PayPa1` skeleton case, but no Cf character appears anywhere in the file's tests.

## Disclosure

The prepared Rust probe (`probe_laneb_test.rs`, same probe folder: asserts Cf names are refused by `normalize_name` and that the BUG-A spoof is refused by `set()`) was **NOT executed this run** — the laptop is unreachable (ongoing fleet-wide SSH outage) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage: run the probe first; it should currently fail on the BUG asserts. The line trace and the premise mirror above are the evidence this filing rests on.

## Why it matters

Petnames are a trust surface: they are how a viewer tells contacts apart when account names are self-asserted ("Account names are alleged"). An invisible-character spoof defeats the one check standing between an alleged name and a look-alike petname, and a bidi override in a label can misrender who is who. The fix is small and local to `petname.rs`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `normalize_name` refuses (or strips, with the choice pinned and documented) Unicode format characters (category Cf) — at minimum U+200B, U+202E/U+202A–U+202E, U+2060, U+FEFF, U+00AD — so the "no control characters" promise matches what callers and readers believe it says.
- [ ] The confusability comparison in `set()` cannot be bypassed by invisible characters: `PayPal`+ZWSP against alleged `PayPal` is refused (by the normalize refusal, an explicit Cf-strip in `fold`/`skeleton`, or both — triage pins which layer owns it).
- [ ] Tests cover at least: ZWSP suffix spoof vs an alleged name, RLO inside a name, and a Cf character against an existing petname (not only against alleged names).
- [ ] Existing petname tests still pass; legitimate names with ordinary punctuation/spaces are unaffected.

## Finding

PR #3058 (merged `facf6481b5`, for #1674) added `is_format_char` in `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/petname.rs` — a hand-listed range set whose doc comment claims "Ranges are the Cf set of Unicode 16". The set is incomplete: **U+061C ARABIC LETTER MARK is category Cf (since Unicode 7) and is not in the list.**

Verified live on current main (`c3fda1c4e6327f7d4e9824608e77fd6461ab0075`): `is_format_char` at `petname.rs:244-266` covers `0600–0605`, `06DD`, `070F`, `0890–0891`, `08E2`, … — no `061C` entry anywhere in the function.

## Why it matters

U+061C is an invisible bidi control — exactly the spoof/reorder class #1674 and #3058 set out to close (the PR's own pinned cases use U+200B and U+202E). Because the set is shared, the gap reaches every consumer:

- `normalize_name` (`petname.rs:293`) accepts a petname carrying U+061C;
- the fold/skeleton comparison path strips only listed Cf, so a stored or alleged name carrying U+061C does not compare by what it renders as;
- invite names reuse the same function (`pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:43`, via PR #3759), so an invite name carrying U+061C also passes.

Dedupe (2026-11-01): searches for `061C` and for petname Cf completeness return only unrelated width/cursor issues (#2962, #1833) and the broader Cf-contract design #3455 — no issue covers this missing code point in `is_format_char`. #1674 is closed by #3058.

## Acceptance criteria

- `is_format_char('\u{061C}')` returns true; a petname and an invite name carrying U+061C are refused, and the fold/skeleton strip removes it.
- A regression test pins U+061C explicitly (named-codepoint style, matching the existing tests in the PR).
- The doc comment's completeness claim is made true — ideally a test or generation note that checks the hand-listed set against the full Unicode Cf set so the next omission is caught mechanically rather than by review.
- Existing petname/invite tests keep passing.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PR #3058's diff against the Unicode Cf set.

items.body:
Design (design-architect pass 31, 2026-11-01). Full design doc: `files/designs/code-id-plain-output-rendering.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited at origin/main `70c20625`. No `user/review`: every origin carries explicit acceptance with a verified probe, and the judgment calls below (one shared character set; escape vs strip by surface kind) are the architect's recorded decisions.

## Summary

pkgs/id's plain-text ruling (#1613, recorded in `src/commands/text.rs`'s module doc) is *a printer never lets a value break row structure* — but every guard in the family tests `char::is_control()` (category Cc only), so Unicode format characters (category Cf) reach the terminal raw and act on the rendering: bidi overrides/isolates (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069) visually reorder the fields after them, and zero-width characters (U+200B, U+FEFF, U+00AD) make look-alike rows with different bytes — the Trojan-Source class applied to live CLI output. Three surfaces, one class:

- **#2839** — `plain_field` (`commands/text.rs:42-44`): a gossip peer name carrying only U+202E returns byte-identical unquoted; quoted, the override is still raw inside the quotes, before the blob-count/timestamp columns it can falsify.
- **#3111** — the shared `key=value` renderer `text()` (`commands/group.rs:64-72`; group/doc/claim via `tokens()`): Cf is raw in both paths — the trigger is `is_whitespace() || is_control()`, and the quoted path is a serde_json literal, which never escapes Cf. Claim values are other nodes' signed tag events (ingest checks length + NFC only; Cf is NFC-stable) sitting before the row's real `author=`/`event=` fields.
- **#3089** — `id world list`'s plain branch (`commands/world.rs:683`) prints host-supplied world names verbatim (neither renderer used): a newline forges a fully-formed extra row, a tab forges columns. Names arrive from a host's wire reply with no validation; #1613's ruling exists precisely for non-conforming hosts.

The character set already exists in-tree, stated once: `petname.rs:237-262` `is_format_char` is the complete Unicode 16 Cf range set, with the doc ruling that Cf characters "are invisible or reorder the text around them" — petnames refuse them at ingest (#1674), but the definition is a private fn the renderers never saw. `world/util.rs:69-84`'s sanitizers (`sanitize_display_name`/`sanitize_chat`) share the `is_control`-only blind spot one layer down.

## The contract (recorded decisions)

> **A plain-text field is row-safe only if it contains no character that can act on the terminal: no structure character (Cc controls, U+2028/U+2029) and no format character (category Cf, the crate's one shared set). Every plain renderer in pkgs/id accounts for both classes; the disposition differs by surface kind — row renderers escape, stripping sanitizers strip, ingest validators refuse — and no surface re-derives the character set.**

1. **One set: the petname set, shared.** `is_format_char` is promoted to a single `pub(crate)` definition all phases use. It includes the zero-width characters #2839 left to triage (U+200B–U+200D, U+FEFF, U+00AD, U+2060): #3111's look-alike argument covers them, and a renderer-specific subset is the per-site re-derivation this design stops. Recorded cost: a ZWJ-emoji or ZWNJ-joined name renders quoted-with-escapes in row renderers — content preserved in full, JSON-parseable — and petnames already refuse these characters outright. Reversible in one place if fleet evidence shows real names harmed.
2. **Escape, don't strip, at row renderers; the two renderers stay distinct.** Their trigger asymmetries are deliberate (space quotes in `key=value`, never in TSV). Cf joins each trigger and is rendered `\uXXXX` inside quotes (`plain_field`'s existing form). For `group::text` the quoted path must escape Cf itself — serde_json's `to_string()` alone never will; that escaping is Phase 2's real work, not the trigger widening. Ordinary values render byte-identically; `--json` unchanged everywhere.
3. **The printer, not ingest.** No new ingest validation for peer names, claim values or world names — #1613's ruling and #3089's non-conforming-host model make rendering the only total gate. Existing ingest checks stay as they are; the closing audit dispositions them separately.

Alternatives rejected in the doc: fixing the three sites independently as filed (the pattern that produced the family — #3111 exists because #2839's fix wouldn't touch its code); one unified renderer (trigger semantics genuinely differ; the shared artefact is the set + contract); stripping at renderers (destroys the printed-in-full, JSON-recoverable property and makes different values print identically); refusing at ingest as the primary fix (cannot clean stored values or non-conforming hosts; refusing other nodes' signed claim events is a federation decision); a bidi-only subset (misses the look-alike half, creates a second drifting set).

## Phases (adopted origins — no parallel issues)

- **Phase 1** = #2839 (`plain_field` honours Cf; creates the shared set + `text.rs` doc truth-up; lands first).
- **Phase 2** = #3111 (`group::text` honours Cf, incl. escaping inside the quoted path; gated on Phase 1 for the shared set definition only).
- **Phase 3a** = #3089 (world list plain branch routes the name through `plain_field`; marker comparison stays on the raw name; not gated — correct today for structure characters, Cf coverage arrives with Phase 1).
- **Phase 3b** = closing inventory + contract statement (filed as a sub-issue, gated on Phases 1–2): every remaining `is_control`-only guard in `pkgs/id/src` dispositioned escape / strip / refuse / deliberately-local with reason — starting population includes the `world/util.rs` sanitizers (expected: strip-Cf for `sanitize_display_name`; `sanitize_chat` decided against its downstream rendering), the directory/world/ssh validator sites, and `world_presentation`/`world_session` payload validation (#3265's width mechanism is different and not adopted); contract + the set's home and Unicode version written into the `text.rs` module doc; closing evidence here, including the sibling-audit evidence #2839's acceptance requires.

Open questions stay in the design doc (ingest-side Cf refusal as defence in depth — federation decision, evidence-gated; `sanitize_chat`'s final disposition if ZWJ-stripping would corrupt legitimate chat text; shared-set placement; ANSI/OSC terminal sequences — no filed instance).

Standing-candidate note: passes 28–30 named this family the standing candidate for this pass (displaced once at pass 30 by #3352's cluster, under its stated terms). Same-day clusters assessed and not taken: the aggregator impossible-date family is #2576's already-stated strict-date rule applied per site; the new operator value-option filings #3449/#3415/#3419 are #3352's contract — provider-catalog-sync is already a named candidate in #3353's closing inventory.

items.body:
**Design (design-architect pass 23): reconstruction is admission — validate authority-bearing inputs where they are rebuilt.**

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-reconstruction-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited against origin/main `206f4fd7`.

## Summary

Six issues filed independently in one evening are one defect with six addresses: in `pkgs/id`, data that carries authority is validated when it is created live, and trusted when it is reconstructed — a world journal being restored, an attestation being computed from decoded objects, a manifest being parsed, a schedule cap being checked. The live path enforces invariants (only issued, JOIN-holding participants act; claims answer the agreement they name; a manifest step means what it says); the reconstruction paths enforce almost none of them, so a crafted or corrupted artefact acquires authority the live path would never have granted.

**The recorded rule:** reconstruction is admission. Anywhere `pkgs/id` rebuilds authority-bearing state from stored or supplied data, the rebuilding code validates the same invariants the live path enforces at creation, and refuses (never partially applies, never silently repairs) data that violates them. Corollaries: validate against state you hold, not claims the input makes; unnamed means refused (scope bits, manifest keys, outcomes); the system shape (sequence 0 / participant 0) is not borrowable by authority-carrying entries.

## Evidence (origin/main 206f4fd7)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs` `restore`: the `Committed` arm's only check is sequence continuity, then `commit_prepared` spends by `event.participant_id` with no record lookup (#2894); the `Checkpoint` arm validates ordering/schedules but no author; the `Issued` arm validates digest/parent/expiry/uses but never scopes — unnamed bits and CHAT/INPUT without JOIN restore clean (#2890). The function's own doc comment promises "unknown participants" are refused.
- The live invariants exist: issuance requires JOIN (`core.rs` issuance path, `scopes.contains(WorldScopes::JOIN)`), delegation subsets keep JOIN (`world/mod.rs` `WorldScopes`), admission runs `authorize(token, required)` per act. Restore consults none of it.
- `pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` `compute_state`: signatures (verified by `chain::decode`) prove who signed, not that the agreement is well-formed — `players = [A, A]` computes `Agreed` from one key (#2863), and a claim's free-form `winner` naming a third party computes `Agreed` (#2868).
- `check_schedule_replacing` trusts a caller-supplied `replacing: bool` for the pending-schedule cap restore enforces — a mismatched flag admits a 65th pending schedule and underflows on an empty map (#2882). The ground truth is in `self.schedules`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs`: serde with defaults, no `deny_unknown_fields` — a typo'd grants/ceiling revocation parses clean, plans zero steps, diff says "no drift" (#2876).
- Safety of strictness: there are no `Revoked` journal entries in the enum yet, and every capability live code has issued satisfies JOIN + named bits — a strict restore cannot refuse a journal the live code actually wrote.

## Phases (adopted origins — no parallel issues filed)

- **Phase 1 — journal restore validates authors and scopes.** #2894 (Committed + Checkpoint author check: author issued, holding the scope its kind requires) + #2890 (Issued scope check: named bits only, JOIN required). One seam, the security core. Independent.
- **Phase 2 — attestation agreement validity.** #2863 (players must be distinct, else `Proposed`) + #2868 (claim outcome domain: winner is `None` or one of the two players; out-of-domain claims ignored under the existing non-player rule). Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 — derive-don't-trust + closing audit.** #2882 (schedule predicate derived from `self.schedules`; trusted parameter removed) + #2876 (`deny_unknown_fields` on the manifest's authority-bearing structs) + a closing inventory audit of the remaining reconstruction seams (sandbox snapshot restore, `world_store` restore_program, directory/petname persistence), each dispositioned already-validating / fixed / exempt-with-reason, and the rule written into the restore and attestation module docs.

## Alternatives considered

- Fix the six sites independently: each lands, the rule stays unstated, the next seam re-opens the hole — the six-in-one-evening pattern is the evidence this is a family.
- Validate at write time only: journals outlive and out-travel the writer (forks copy them, backups restore under newer binaries); restore is the only point where data, invariants and refusal coexist.
- Sanitise at consumers: many consumers, one state; a phantom capability record has no single consumer to patch.
- Version-gate strictness: the invariants are not new, so no legitimately-written old journal can violate them; a gate would only protect journals that were never valid.

## Risks / open questions

- Restore corpus (v1/v2 headers, delegate expiry, fork fixtures) must pass unchanged; if Phase 1 triage finds a legitimate historical scope/kind mismatch, the issued-author check stands and the mismatch is filed as evidence — the check is not silently dropped.
- Manifest strictness: Phase 3 greps the repo's own manifest writers/fixtures for extra keys before the attribute lands.
- Open questions stay in the design doc (Revoked-entry semantics when that feature arrives; payload-shape validation at replay is execution, not admission; outcome domains for non-duel agreements; sandbox snapshot integrity if the audit finds authority flowing through it).

Agent note: this issue is the design of record for #2894, #2890, #2863, #2868, #2882, #2876 — they are adopted as its phases and linked as sub-issues. Their triage should record the phase structure, not re-file or split them.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every authority-bearing reconstruction path in `pkgs/id` named by this design (journal restore, attestation computation, manifest parsing, schedule checks) validates the same invariants its live creation path enforces, and refuses — never partially applies, never silently repairs — violating input.
- Each of the six filed instances (#2894, #2890, and the siblings named in the design doc) is either fixed under this contract or explicitly dispositioned against it.
- Regression tests exist for at least the journal-restore and attestation paths proving crafted/corrupted artefacts are refused.
- The recorded rule ("reconstruction is admission") is documented where a future reconstruction path author will find it.

## Problem

`read_journal_entries` — the raw journal reader behind `id world fork` — refuses a crash-torn final entry in a world journal that `FileJournal::open` on the very same file forgives: a world that opens, serves and verifies fine after a crash cannot be forked until someone hand-repairs its journal.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:452-466` — `read_journal_entries` splits the file bytes on `\n` and parses every non-empty chunk with `serde_json::from_slice(...)?` (`{path} is corrupt`). The final chunk after a crash-torn append is an unterminated truncated fragment; it is parsed like any other entry and fails the whole read. There is no torn-tail special case.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` — `FileJournal::open`, the normal open path for the same journal, treats exactly this case as recoverable: an unterminated last line is a torn append (the crash came before the entry was acknowledged), so it is dropped, the file is truncated to `good_len`, and a warning is logged. Only a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption there.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:479` — `fork_world` starts with `read_journal_entries(&src_dir.join("journal.jsonl"))?`. Forking a *cold* world (not currently open — e.g. after the crash that tore the tail, before anything reopens it) therefore fails with `journal.jsonl is corrupt`, even though simply opening that world would have repaired the tail and proceeded.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:190` — the second caller is `FileJournal::append`'s version-bump path (#227), which re-reads the journal through the same helper; it is normally shielded because `open` truncates first, which shows the helper's strictness is an accident of reuse, not a ruling: the fork path has no such shield.
- No test covers `read_journal_entries` / `fork_world` against a journal with an unterminated final fragment.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) covers `Petnames::open`; #1521 / #1522 (filed 2026-10-27) cover the directory journal and the group log. No open or recently-closed issue mentions `read_journal_entries`, `fork_world` and a torn journal tail.

## Why it matters

Forking (F12.2) is the template/backup path for worlds. The scenario where an admin most wants a fork — recovering or cloning a world after a crash — is exactly the scenario where the journal may carry a torn tail, and it is the one path that refuses it while the world's own open path quietly repairs it. The error message (`is corrupt`) also misdiagnoses a torn append as corruption, sending the admin toward discarding a journal that was never corrupt.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `read_journal_entries` (or the fork path) treats a final unterminated fragment the way `FileJournal::open` does: the fragment is excluded from the returned entries (and the exclusion is visible — a warning log or a fork note), so `fork_world` succeeds on a crash-torn source journal and the fork replays to the parent's last complete entry.
- [ ] A newline-terminated unparseable line, anywhere including the last line, still fails with the corrupt-journal error — corruption is never silently dropped.
- [ ] New tests cover: fork of a journal with a torn final fragment (succeeds, fork state = last complete entry), fork of a journal with a complete-but-corrupt final line (fails).
- [ ] `FileJournal::append`'s version-bump caller (#227) behaviour is unchanged for journals it has opened.

## Problem

A crash-torn final line in `groups.jsonl` bricks every group command: `GroupLog::open` refuses the unterminated partial event that a crash mid-append leaves behind, instead of dropping and truncating it the way the sibling JSONL stores in this codebase do.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/groups/log.rs:137-150` — `GroupLog::append` writes one JSON line + `\n` with a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`. A crash/power loss during that write leaves a final line that is a truncated JSON fragment with no terminating newline.
- `pkgs/id/src/groups/log.rs:48-71` — `GroupLog::open` collects `text.lines()` through `serde_json::from_str(...)?` for every non-empty line. `lines()` yields the unterminated final fragment as a line, so one torn append fails the whole open with `line N is not an event`. There is no torn-tail special case: no missing-final-newline check, no truncation/repair.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:200,361,395` — every group command (`cmd_group` and helpers) starts with `GroupLog::open(&log_path(path))?`, so one torn append makes all group operations fail the same way until someone hand-edits `groups.jsonl`.
- Contrast — the established house semantics in the same codebase:
  - `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` (`FileJournal::open`): an unterminated last line is a torn append — dropped, file truncated to the last complete line; a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption and still fails.
  - `pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:143-165` (`Outbox::open`): unterminated failing final line is dropped and the file truncated via `set_len(kept)`; a complete corrupt line still errors.
  - `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:575-600` and `pkgs/id/src/directory_log.rs:196-235`: same drop-the-torn-tail treatment.
- Existing test `test_a_line_that_is_not_an_event_is_an_error` (`groups/log.rs:386-392`) writes `"not json\n"` — a *complete*, newline-terminated line — and correctly asserts an error. No test covers an unterminated final fragment, which is the distinct torn case the sibling stores forgive.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) is the same defect class in `Petnames::open` only (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`); the directory journal instance is filed separately as #1521. No open or recently-closed issue mentions `GroupLog` / `groups.jsonl` torn tails.

## Why it matters

Groups are a user-facing feature whose entire local history lives in this one append-only log. Its own append path can produce exactly the torn tail its load path refuses — so a single ill-timed crash converts a recoverable restart into a permanently unopenable group log, while the envelope outbox written by the same binary already survives the same crash.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GroupLog::open` on a log whose final line is an unterminated truncated fragment loads all complete events, drops the fragment, and truncates the file to the last complete line (mirroring `FileJournal::open` / `Outbox::open` semantics, including a warning log).
- [ ] A newline-terminated line that does not parse, anywhere including the last line, still fails — the existing `test_a_line_that_is_not_an_event_is_an_error` test keeps passing unchanged.
- [ ] New tests cover: torn final fragment (loads + file truncated), torn fragment after valid events (earlier events intact and `projection()` still folds).
- [ ] No change to the event format, the fold, or append behaviour.

## Problem

A crash-torn final line in the directory journal bricks the directory permanently: `Directory::open` / `Directory::replay` refuse the unterminated partial entry that a crash mid-append leaves behind, instead of dropping and truncating it the way the sibling JSONL stores in this codebase do.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:527-543` — `Directory::append` writes one JSON line + `\n` with a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`. A crash/power loss during that write leaves a final line that is a truncated JSON fragment with no terminating newline.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:505-525` — `Directory::replay` iterates `text.lines()` (which yields the unterminated final fragment as a line) and propagates any parse failure with `?` at `:516-517` (`directory journal line N is malformed`). There is no torn-tail special case: no check for a missing final newline, no truncation/repair.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:471-473` — `Directory::open` (the production load path) is `Self::replay(path)?` first, so one torn append makes every subsequent open fail the same way; the directory never recovers without manual file surgery.
- Contrast — the established house semantics in the same codebase:
  - `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` (`FileJournal::open`): an unterminated last line is a torn append — dropped, file truncated to `good_len`, with a comment explaining that a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption and must still fail.
  - `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:575-600` (`ArtifactLog::open` — the very log `Directory::open` loads immediately after the journal): drops and truncates a final line cut short by a crash.
  - `pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:143-165` and `pkgs/id/src/directory_log.rs:196-235`: same drop-the-torn-tail treatment.
- Existing test `replay_rebuilds_the_directory_and_refuses_a_broken_journal` (`directory.rs:2601`) covers an *apply-refused* complete entry, not a torn tail; no test covers an unterminated final fragment.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) is the same defect class in `Petnames::open` only (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`); it names FileJournal and Outbox as the good examples and does not cover the directory journal. No open or recently-closed issue mentions the directory journal / `Directory::replay` torn tail.

## Why it matters

The directory journal is the durable record of accounts, friendships and group membership for the directory service. Its own append path can produce exactly the torn tail its load path refuses — so a single ill-timed crash converts a recoverable restart into a permanently unopenable directory, while the artifact log sitting next to it (loaded in the same `open`) already survives the same crash.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Directory::replay`/`open` on a journal whose final line is an unterminated truncated fragment loads all complete entries, drops the fragment, and truncates the file to the last complete line (mirroring `FileJournal::open` / `ArtifactLog::open` semantics, including a warning log).
- [ ] A newline-terminated line that does not parse, anywhere including the last line, still fails with the existing `directory journal line N is malformed` error — corruption is never silently dropped.
- [ ] A complete entry that `apply` refuses still fails replay (existing test at `directory.rs:2601` keeps passing).
- [ ] New tests cover: torn final fragment (loads + file truncated), complete-but-corrupt final line (errors), torn fragment after valid entries (earlier entries intact).

items.body:
## Problem

`ColdStore._write_private_json` (pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py:373-378) writes `credentials.json` and `state.json` **in place**: `os.open(path, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC)` followed by `json.dump` directly into the destination file. There is no temp file, no `os.replace`, and no fsync. A crash, power loss, OOM kill, or any exception mid-`json.dump` leaves the destination truncated to a partial JSON document.

Both readers then fail hard with a **raw** error, not the module's own error type:

- `load_state` (cold_store.py:393-396) does a bare `json.loads(self.state_path.read_text())` — a torn `state.json` raises `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` uncaught. `load_state` is on the path of `ensure_folders` (:687) and `_folder_id`/`_d1_endpoint` (:709, :1242), so one torn write wedges every later run until a human hand-repairs the file.
- `load_credentials` (cold_store.py:381-391) does the same bare `json.loads` — a torn `credentials.json` raises raw `JSONDecodeError` instead of the `ColdStoreError("credentials.json is missing …")`-style actionable errors the function otherwise raises, masking the real cause (the file exists; it is half-written).

`save_state` (cold_store.py:398-405) is called on routine paths (e.g. after folder discovery, :705), so the exposure window is every run, not just `init`.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-31)

Code: cold_store.py:373-378 (in-place O_TRUNC write), :381-396 (bare `json.loads` in both loaders), :398-405 (`save_state` via the same writer).

Laptop probe (source sha-matched: cold_store.py sha256 `fba42e08027514abae2de1602e755854ebfd6a3b578a5eece34b6c0becd39b95` on both sandbox main `ed3a285e` and the laptop copy; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-coldstore-atomic/`):

- Control: `save_state({"folders": {"a": "1"}})` then `load_state()` returns the dict.
- Simulated crash mid-write (partial JSON flushed, then the write aborts): `state.json` is left as `b'{"folders": {"a": "1"'`.
- After that, `load_state()` **raises `JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 22`** — and `isinstance(e, ColdStoreError)` is `False`.
- Same simulation against `_write_private_json(credentials_path, …)`: `load_credentials()` raises the same raw `JSONDecodeError`.

Contrast within the same repo: pkgs/id's JSONL stores treat a crash-torn tail as a normal, repairable case (e.g. `Petnames::open` drops and truncates a torn final line). Cold-store's two most state-critical JSON files get no such protection.

## Why it matters

Cold-store is the backup system: its `state.json` carries the Drive folder map every backup/restore run depends on, and `credentials.json` is hand-filled from Bitwarden — a torn credentials file destroyed by a crash during an unrelated `save_state`-adjacent write forces manual credential re-entry. A backup tool whose own state files are the least crash-safe part of the system will eventually wedge a nightly run with an inscrutable stdlib traceback instead of an actionable error.

## Distinct from

- #3240 (github-backup's plan/state/MANIFEST non-atomic writes — different tool, different files).
- #2550 (prune_backups Drive/ledger crash-consistency — remote side, not the local JSON writers).
- #940 (closed; token cached in state.json + file permissions — not write atomicity).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_write_private_json` writes to a temp file in the same directory, fsyncs, and `os.replace`s onto the destination (preserving 0600), so a crash at any point leaves either the old or the new complete document.
- [ ] `load_state` / `load_credentials` on a corrupt file raise `ColdStoreError` naming the file and the parse problem (or recover to a documented default), never a raw `JSONDecodeError`.
- [ ] Regression test: simulate a mid-write failure (partial write + raise) and assert the previous complete document still loads, for both state and credentials paths.
- [ ] Existing cold-store test suite passes.

items.body:
## Problem

`Outbox::open` (`pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:130`) only drops a torn final line when it **fails to parse**. A crash that cuts an append after the record's closing `}` but before its `\n` leaves a *parseable* unterminated final line — and `open` accepts it as a committed record. The next `commit()` then appends the following record directly onto that same line, producing one line containing two JSON objects; on the next open that line is complete (newline-terminated) and corrupt, so `open` errors out and the envelope outbox is bricked until a human edits the file by hand.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `1658679c`)

- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:141-157`: the replay loop iterates `text.split_inclusive('\n')`; on parse success it applies the record and does `kept += line.len()` (line 146) **regardless of whether the line ends with `\n`**. The torn-tail drop is only the `Err(_) if !complete => break` arm (line 148). If the unterminated fragment parses, `kept == text.len()`, so no truncation happens and the file keeps its missing trailing newline.
- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:278-289` (`commit`): appends `serde_json::to_string(&record) + '\n'` with `OpenOptions::append` — no leading newline is written, so the next record is concatenated onto the unterminated line.
- Sibling stores treat *any* unterminated final line as torn, parseable or not, because an append that never got its newline was never durably committed:
  - `src/artifact.rs:565-583` (`ArtifactLog::open`): "A final line cut short by a crash was never synced, so it is dropped and the file is truncated to the last complete line" — implemented as `rfind('\n')` truncation *before* parsing.
  - `src/directory.rs:512-526` (the #1521 fix): drops the torn final fragment "parseable or not", warns, and truncates.
- The existing test `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record` (`src/envelope_outbox.rs:523`) covers only an *unparseable* fragment (`{"op":"queued","target"`). The parseable-fragment case — its exact title scenario, "not mixed into the next record" — is untested and currently fails by construction: fragment `{"op":"queued",...}` + appended record = `{"op":...}{"op":...}\n`, which no longer parses as a single record (demonstrated with a JSON parse of the concatenated line this run).
- Accepting the fragment also breaks the durability contract: `commit` does `write_all` then `sync_data` (line 285-288); a crash between the data write and the sync can leave exactly this parseable-but-unterminated tail for a record that was never acknowledged.

## Why it matters

The outbox is the durable delivery queue for envelopes/artifacts. One unlucky crash turns it into a file that loads once (silently accepting an unacknowledged record), then permanently fails to load after the next enqueue/withdraw/record — with a "line N is corrupt" error that gives no hint the real cause was a torn tail two restarts earlier.

Related but distinct: #1499 (petnames) and #1522 (groups) cite the Outbox as the *correct* sibling for refusing torn tails; neither covers this parseable-unterminated acceptance in the Outbox itself. #1521 (directory, closed) established the "drop parseable or not" policy this issue asks the Outbox to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Outbox::open` drops an unterminated final line **whether or not it parses**, truncates the file to the last complete (newline-terminated) line, matching `ArtifactLog::open` / directory replay semantics.
- [ ] After such a recovery, a subsequent `commit()` appends cleanly: reopening the outbox succeeds and contains exactly the pre-crash complete records plus the new one.
- [ ] A corrupt *complete* (newline-terminated) line still fails the load (existing test `a_corrupt_complete_line_stops_the_load` keeps passing).
- [ ] New regression test: final line is a complete JSON record missing only its trailing `\n`; open drops it (the record's envelope is not present), the file is truncated, a following enqueue round-trips through a reopen.
- [ ] Existing outbox tests pass, including `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record`.
